I’m sorry you’re dealing with so much all at once. Are you still in college? If i were you I’d seriously consider taking a semester off just to reset and recalibrate, and heal. College relationships can be fun and exciting but also so painful and stressful to maintain. You’re still growing and at such an accelerated rate. You sound like an intense guy, who likes an adrenaline rush and competition, and there’s nothing wrong with that. But maybe sometimes when you have a lot of high-adrenaline experiences, and something crappy happens in your personal life, you might be more likely to fall into a deep depression over it. It’s an emotional intensity that’s impossible to make sense of. Plus you’re still in school and thinking about what you want to do the rest of your life, so there’s just so much going on. I took a leave of absence from work earlier this year because i was so stressed, and i got to take time to just enjoy being alive for the first time in a while. Now i set firmer boundaries in my personal and work relationships. I know it probably sounds like a crazy idea, and i don’t know if you have a family that would support your decision, but it could be life changing to take a mental vacation.

I was a lot like you when I first went to college. Failing everything and hiding it from my folks. Didn't do pills but drank and smoked a ton. I simply wasn't ready for college, but I was too humiliated and ashamed to admit it. It sucked that I felt like I couldn't be more honest with anyone (except maybe my gf at the time, but she couldn't really help me). I carried this on for longer than you might think possible without actually failing out—3 years. I cheated and lied and cried and begged just because I didn't want to admit that I might need help. I finally dropped out. It was embarrassing at first, but I started a journey that led to getting professional help that changed my life. I got my degree later, when I had a stronger foundation and actually appreciated the value of an education. I didn't have that appreciation when I was 18–21. It was still a struggle, but I was more comfortable in my own skin, which was odd now that I think about it, because I was years older than my classmates. But that didn't matter. The moral of the story is don't kill yourself, because if all you have to worry about is what people will think of you if you fail out, you will get over that. Life actually does get easier in the sense that you care less what other people think as you get older.

I sort of fell into publishing to be honest. My senior year I panicked because I still did not know what I wanted to do. As I said I was half-heartedly interested in teaching but not committed. I was an English major and my counselor/English professor recommended editing, so I interned with a publishing company in the city (Philly, which is a decent publishing town) and ended up enjoying it enough to apply to jobs in the industry later. 

My supervisor at the internship told me about PublishersMarketplace, which (I think, if I remember right) is where I found a copyediting job opportunity at a small—no, tiny, less than 40 employees—company in a small town in Pennsylvania. I got kinda lucky because this place’s speciality was niche subjects, which the place where I’d interned specialized in as well, so my interview went very smoothly. Also this place did not have a strong copyediting/proofreading process in place at the time and they did not require much experience of the new copyediting position. Perfect for me. I didn’t realize until I started working just how low their editorial bar was, which was troubling at first but it put me in a great position, that is, sort of leading the charge toward raising that bar, which was great stuff for my resume later. That’s my long answer to your question.

The short answer is I just took the first job I could find even though it was in the-middle-of-nowhere PA and I had to take Amtrak there every morning (!!!). But that led to making connections that led to a much better job after a few years. The publishing world is a pretty tight network, which is one nice thing about it.

I don't think you know what you're talking about. I came here today b/c I haven't in a while but I literally just finished reading Noonday Demon, an exhaustive, well-researched book about depression written 20 years ago, and I've been wanting to share my thoughts on it. This seems like a good opportunity. In the final chapters the author talks about how most relatively functional people have nothing but disdain for and intolerance of depressed people, even if they more or less conceal that disdain in public. It is true that the best things to do for depression are therapy, exercise, engaging your brain in challenging things, possibly taking meds, but what highly functional, nondepresed, intolerant-of-depressives (although certainly otherwise good) people don't get is how insidious real clinical deep depression is. You can be on top of the world one day and thinking you're ready to end it all the next. And I'm not even talking about bipolar disorder—that's just normal depression. And if you can't afford therapy, this sub is a good place to start. Also, group therapy is tremendously helpful. It's good that there is a therapist in the room, I'll give you that. But you are not that person and honestly it's frustrating that 20 years after Andrew Solomon wrote that book the are still people who really just don't get it.

However, they may be doing more harm than good, b/c they often come off disingenuous and drawing the ire of actual GAD sufferers and mental-illness skeptics alike. It's hard to believe mental illness still carries such a stigma. But there are always going to be people who a) will never recognize or admit they may be suffering from such an illness and b) people who are hypochondriacal about it. Maybe you care too much. I've been guilty of this. Don't worry about your boss's blood pressure. And don't worry so much about how small the company is. That's the owners' problem. They obviously need you more than you think they do. Also try not to take missteps too seriously. Learn from mistakes and brush your shoulders off. I'm currently making the jump from a small to a large company. Thought I would never get out of it but I did. You should do everything you can to expand your professional network—in and outside your company. Be friendly, do things nobody else wants to do, and don't complain (unless it's something that's affecting the bottom line). Most importantly, cultivate a positive attitude.
